items.title: Two Sum: do number jinka jod target ho, ek pass mein
items.one_idea: Two Sum: for each number ask whether its partner (target minus the number) was already seen; a hash map answers that in one step, so one pass over the list replaces checking every pair.
items.spoken_hook: List में दो number, जिनका जोड़ 11{ग्यारह} हो, कैसे ढूँढें?
items.hook_source: direct_question: the problem itself as a plain question, no term used before it is explained (owner 2026-10-22); hookscore to run on the Roman form in the script step
items.hook_10s: List में दो number, जिनका जोड़ 11{ग्यारह} हो, कैसे ढूँढें? List है 5, 1, 12, 3, 8. हर जोड़ी जाँचो तो 10{दस} checks लगते हैं, पर एक तरीका सिर्फ़ 5{पाँच} steps में बता देता है। [frame 0: five cells 5 1 12 3 8 in a row, a gold chip 11 above; two cells glow-free highlighted by a bracket joining 3 and 8]

hook_candidates.text: List में दो number, जिनका जोड़ 11{ग्यारह} हो, कैसे ढूँढें?
पाँच करोड़ जोड़ियाँ जाँचने की जगह, दस हज़ार numbers में सिर्फ़ दस हज़ार steps।
Interviewer ने पूछा: list में कौन-से दो number जुड़कर दिया हुआ target बनाते हैं?

items.visual_idea: A row of five cells (5 1 12 3 8) with a target chip 11. Brute force: arcs link every pair one after another with a counter climbing to 10, then crossed out in red. Then a walking pointer visits each cell; a small two-column table (number, index) fills one row per step, and at cell 8 an arrow computes 11 minus 8 equals 3, jumps to the table row for 3 and the two cells get joined by a bracket.
items.everyday_anchor: At a wedding buffet two friends want plates that together cost exactly 11 rupees of coupons; instead of trying every friend with every friend, you note each person's coupon in a notebook as they walk by and ask whether the missing amount is already written there.
items.example: EXAMPLE list [5, 1, 12, 3, 8] with target 11; answer indices [3, 4] (3 + 8). Run: brute force 10 checks, one pass 5 steps. For 10,000 numbers: 49,995,000 pair checks (all pairs) vs 10,000 steps.
items.pattern: complement lookup with a hash map (remember what you have seen; ask for the partner in one step)
items.pattern_signal: For every item you need to know if a matching partner already exists somewhere earlier in the data: that is a lookup question, so a hash map fits.
items.beats: hook and problem 10s; brute force pairs crossed out with run counts 14s; pattern, signal and insight (target minus x is the partner) 18s; code in 4 sub-steps with real output 38s; complexity O(n) time O(n) space plus the trap (look before you store, so a number never pairs with itself, [3,3] target 6) 18s; check yourself and follow 10s
items.check_question: List [2, 7, 11, 15], target 26: which indices? (answer [2,3], 11 + 15; in the caption)
facts_to_verify: Problem paraphrase from the doocs mirror of the LeetCode Two Sum statement (leetcode.com itself returned 403 to WebFetch this session): array of integers and a target, return the indices of two entries summing to target; exactly one answer; same element not used twice; any index order; 2 to 10^4 elements; values -10^9 to 10^9. Re-check against the problem page if it becomes reachable.
Hash table one-pass solution: O(n) time, O(n) space, check the partner before inserting the current number (doocs page, fetched).
Average O(1) lookup and worst case O(n) for a hash table (Wikipedia Hash table complexity table, fetched); say 'average O(1)', never promise worst case.

Run the code and show its real output: brute force on [5,1,12,3,8] target 11 -> ([3, 4], 10 checks); one pass -> [3, 4] after 5 steps; [3,3] target 6 -> [0, 1]; n=10000 all pairs = 49995000 (run this session by the strategist, builder re-runs).
